lessons.transfer: Recalculate the result with one changed assumption, document the effect and justify the next evidence request.

lessons.title: Capital staging and stop-loss gates
body: Staged investment preserves the option to abandon. Compare a $5M pilot plus contingent $25M expansion with a single $30M commitment by measuring probabilities, information quality, and delay costs. Do not count hypothetical upside as guaranteed.
Executive application: distinguish disclosed facts from hypothetical inputs. Identify a counterargument, a practical risk, and a measurable signal that would justify changing this recommendation.
lessons.example: A pilot is justified by the expected improvement in future decisions less its cost and delay, not by a positive narrative alone.
lessons.transfer: Recalculate the result with one changed assumption, document the effect and justify the next evidence request.

lessons.title: Debt equity and dilution
body: Funding choice changes risk, governance and future flexibility. At $40M pre-money valuation and a $10M new common-equity investment, simplified post-money valuation is $50M; the new investor owns 20% when no other rights or options intervene.
Managerial challenge: explain which input is observed versus assumed, identify a sensitivity and request the evidence necessary to act.
lessons.example: Investor ownership=10/(40+10)=20%; prior holders collectively retain 80%.
lessons.transfer: Replace a major assumption and recalculate. Explain whether your recommendation reverses and why.

lessons.title: Financing runway and covenant constraints
body: A venture with $25M unrestricted cash and $3M net monthly cash burn has 8.33 months of arithmetic runway before a cash floor. At a $7M minimum cash floor, usable runway is 6 months. Funding must be planned before the breach, including lead time and contingencies.
Managerial challenge: explain which input is observed versus assumed, identify a sensitivity and request the evidence necessary to act.
lessons.example: Usable cash=25−7=18; 18/3=6 months. This model assumes steady monthly burn.
lessons.transfer: Replace a major assumption and recalculate. Explain whether your recommendation reverses and why.

lessons.title: Build a board-ready numerical bridge
body: Founders own 100% before Series A. New investors contribute $15M for 30% post-money ordinary shares with no option pools or special terms.
Post-money=15/.30=50M; pre-money=35M. Founders own 70% after round. A subsequent round may dilute founders again.
Reconcile each input, mark the simplifications, identify the budget, cash and governance constraints, and explain why a favorable average need not imply an acceptable downside.
lessons.example: Post-money=15/.30=50M; pre-money=35M. Founders own 70% after round. A subsequent round may dilute founders again.
lessons.transfer: Change two of the stated numerical inputs by 10% in opposite directions. Recalculate all outputs. Explain how uncertainty changes your decision.

lessons.title: Demand, supply and opportunity cost
body: Demand describes quantities buyers would purchase at different prices, holding other influences constant. Supply describes quantities sellers would offer. A change in the product’s price moves along a curve; a change in income, preferences, input costs or technology can shift a curve. Confusing a shift with a movement produces faulty causal explanations.

Equilibrium in the simple competitive model is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. Solve both equations in the same units and domain. The intersection is a model prediction under assumptions, not an assertion that every real market clears instantly. Contracts, capacity, search and regulation can delay adjustment.

Opportunity cost is the value of the best forgone alternative. An owned warehouse still has an economic cost if it could be leased to another company. Sunk expenditures are different: they cannot be recovered and do not change between future choices. Economic profit subtracts explicit and implicit opportunity costs.

A binding price ceiling below equilibrium creates excess demand in the basic model; a floor above equilibrium creates excess supply. Distributional and dynamic effects need additional analysis. For a corporation, a commodity supply disruption shifts costs and may change both market price and quantity. Identify the affected market before transferring a conclusion to the whole economy.
lessons.example: Demand Qd = 100 − 2P and supply Qs = 20 + 2P. Equate: 100 − 2P = 20 + 2P, so P = 20 and Q = 60. A demand shift to Qd = 120 − 2P gives P = 25 and Q = 70. At a ceiling P = 15 under original curves, Qd = 70 and Qs = 50, a shortage of 20.
lessons.transfer: Solve the original demand with new supply Qs = 2P. Explain the price and quantity change as an adverse supply shift.

lessons.title: Price sensitivity and market power
body: Price elasticity of demand measures percentage quantity response to percentage price change. For discrete comparisons, the midpoint method divides each change by the average of its starting and ending values. Demand elasticity is usually negative; label whether you report the signed value or its absolute magnitude. Elasticity varies by product, horizon and location on a demand curve.

With elastic demand, a small price increase tends to lower revenue; with inelastic demand it tends to raise revenue, other things equal. Profit still depends on costs. Do not infer an optimal price from elasticity alone when competition, capacity and contracts matter. A correlation in historical prices and sales is not a controlled demand experiment.

Marginal analysis compares additional benefit with additional cost. A price-taking firm uses market price as marginal revenue; a firm facing downward-sloping demand generally has marginal revenue below price because selling more may require lowering price. Introductory profit maximization uses MR = MC at an appropriate interior maximum, subject to feasibility and relevant shutdown conditions.

Market power can arise from differentiation, switching costs, networks, scarce assets or legal barriers. Accounting margins alone do not prove durable power. Ask whether substitutes, entry, buyer bargaining or innovation can erode returns. Competitive and regulatory responses belong in the decision case.
lessons.example: Price rises from 10 to 12 and quantity falls from 100 to 80. Midpoint quantity change is −20/90 = −22.22%; midpoint price change is 2/11 = 18.18%; elasticity is −1.22. Revenue falls from 1,000 to 960. If variable cost is 6 per unit, contribution rises from 400 to 480, so revenue and contribution point in different directions.
lessons.transfer: Recompute contribution with unit variable cost 2. Explain why the same demand response can imply a different profit recommendation.

lessons.title: Inflation, interest rates and currency
body: Inflation is a rise in the general price level, not proof that every company can raise every price. Real growth adjusts nominal growth for price changes: real factor = nominal factor divided by price-level factor. For larger changes use the exact ratio rather than simply subtracting rates. Corporate exposure depends on input contracts, pricing power and customer income.

Interest rates affect borrowing costs, asset values, investment hurdles and customer demand. Fixed-rate debt does not reprice immediately, while variable-rate debt and refinancing create transmission channels. A rate shock can coincide with recession or exchange-rate changes; isolate mechanisms before combining them into scenarios.

Currency changes affect translation of foreign financial statements, transactions and competitiveness differently. State the quotation convention. If one foreign-currency unit buys fewer dollars, a foreign sale translates to fewer dollars before hedging or operational offsets. Foreign costs may offset part of the revenue exposure. Translation losses are not automatically equivalent to a cash outflow.

Build a scenario matrix by business unit: revenue volumes, selling prices, input prices, interest exposure and working-capital effects. A macro forecast is uncertain. Use scenario ranges and identify leading indicators, timing and contractual offsets. Do not infer company earnings directly from a single GDP statistic.
lessons.example: Nominal sales rise 8% while relevant prices rise 5%; approximate real volume/value growth under this simple deflator is 1.08/1.05 − 1 = 2.86%. Floating debt of 400 million exposed to a 2-percentage-point rate rise adds 8 million annual interest before offsets. Foreign sales of 100 million units translate from 120 to 110 million dollars if the rate falls from $1.20 to $1.10 per unit.
lessons.transfer: Construct a recession scenario for an exporter with local costs and foreign revenues. Identify at least one offset and one lag.

lessons.title: Elasticity, marginal revenue and pricing
body: When a firm faces downward-sloping demand, selling an additional unit can require lowering price on existing units. For linear inverse demand P=a−bQ with constant marginal cost c, total revenue is aQ−bQ² and marginal revenue is a−2bQ. The interior profit maximum sets marginal revenue equal to marginal cost when a>c, capacity permits and the second-order shape is appropriate.

This is a model, not a prescription to maximize price. Contracts, competitive responses, quality, product interactions and regulation can invalidate the simple demand curve. Evidence on demand often comes from controlled tests or natural variation, not from a single before/after observation with changing macro conditions.

Price elasticity varies along a linear demand curve. At the interior monopoly optimum with constant marginal cost, the absolute elasticity exceeds one when marginal cost is positive under the standard model. A high margin does not establish market power without substitutes and entry analysis. A board decision should include customer welfare, reputation and long-run incentives as well as a one-period profit calculation.
lessons.example: Fictional inverse demand P=100−Q, Q measured in thousands and price in dollars; unit marginal cost 20 and fixed cost 1,000 thousand dollars. Revenue in thousands is 100Q−Q²; MR=100−2Q. MR=MC=20 gives Q=40 thousand and P=60; contribution before fixed cost is (60−20)×40=1,600 thousand; profit=600 thousand. At Q=50, P=50, profit is 500 thousand.
lessons.transfer: Find revenue-maximizing quantity and compare it with profit-maximizing quantity. Explain why a revenue bonus could distort the decision.

lessons.title: Strategic commitments and sequential competition
body: A game model identifies players, available actions, payoffs and information. A dominant strategy yields a higher payoff regardless of the rival’s action; a Nash equilibrium is a pair where neither player gains by changing alone. Those concepts differ. One observed outcome does not establish a durable equilibrium if payoffs or information change.

Sequential games require backward induction. If a rival promises to match every discount, ask whether matching is optimal after a discount is actually observed. An incredible threat cannot discipline the first mover in a rational model. Capacity investments, contracts or public commitments may change incentives, but can also be costly or legally restricted.

A pricing committee should map at least two rival responses and customer-switching assumptions. A small static payoff table can teach strategic thinking but cannot predict a real industry without evidence on entry, costs, contracts and regulation. For real firms, seek qualified competition-law review before any coordinated behavior or information exchange.
lessons.example: Two firms choose Hold or Cut. Payoffs (A,B): Hold/Hold=(8,8); Cut/Hold=(11,3); Hold/Cut=(3,11); Cut/Cut=(5,5). Each firm prefers Cut against either rival choice, so Cut/Cut is the unique dominant-strategy Nash equilibrium, even though both would earn 8 from Hold/Hold. This table is fictional and is not permission to coordinate prices.
lessons.transfer: Change Cut/Cut payoffs to (2,2). Identify whether Cut is still dominant and what additional information would be needed to predict behavior in a repeated market.

lessons.title: Macro shock transmission and pricing power
body: A macro scenario should connect rates, inflation, currencies and demand through separately documented channels. Nominal revenue growth mixes quantity, price and currency translation. If local-currency unit sales rise, the dollar result can still fall when translation weakens. A firm with imported inputs may have an offsetting cost effect; the net exposure requires matching currencies and contracts.

Fixed-rate debt is protected from immediate repricing but can face a maturity wall. Floating debt may reprice after reset, while a hedge can postpone or reshape the cash effect. Higher discount rates may reduce investment values even before current interest expense changes. State the time horizon and rate convention before adding exposures.

Use a coherent bear case: demand falls, receivable days rise and funding gets more expensive together. Calculate revenue, contribution, interest and cash timing separately. Adding percentage shocks to dollars without a common base is invalid. Decision options include hedging contracted currency cash, changing product mix and staging capital expenditure, each with costs and limits.
lessons.example: A foreign subsidiary sells 100 million units of foreign currency annually, with 60 million units of local costs. Exchange falls from $1.20 to $1.10 per foreign unit: translated revenue falls 10 million dollars, but translated local cost falls 6 million, so pre-tax operating contribution falls 4 million before volume or hedges. Floating debt 200 million dollars resetting +2 percentage points adds 4 million annual interest if fully exposed.
lessons.transfer: Add a 10% foreign-currency sales decline while costs are 80% variable in the short run. Build the revised dollar contribution and distinguish it from cash collection.

lessons.title: Build a currency, tariff and rate earnings bridge
body: An executive should not convert a monetary-policy announcement directly into a forecast of company earnings. Map channels and timing: a policy-rate change may reprice floating debt quickly, influence demand and currency with uncertain lags, and affect domestic input costs differently from imported components. Inflation is a change in a price index, not necessarily the exact increase in a company’s costs. A tariff is applied to the relevant customs value under the stated trade assumption, not automatically to all sales.

Fictional Meridian sells 120 million dollars domestically and 80 million euros abroad. It buys domestic inputs for 90 million dollars, imported components for 50 million euros and has 25 million dollars fixed operating cost. At 1.10 dollars per euro, revenue is 208, operating cost is 90+55+25=170 and EBIT is 38 million dollars. Floating debt 200 million at 5% costs 10 interest; with a 25% tax assumption and full use of deductions, net income is (38−10)×.75=21.

In a correlated downside, the euro falls to 1.00 dollar, domestic input cost rises 6%, an illustrative 8% tariff applies to the dollar customs value of imported components, and the floating rate becomes 7%. Revenue is 120+80=200. Operating cost is 95.4+50+4 tariff+25=174.4; EBIT is 25.6. Interest is 14; net income is (25.6−14)×.75=8.7. The EBIT bridge is −3 on net euro receipts, −5.4 domestic input inflation and −4 tariff, or −12.4 in total. The extra 4 interest is below EBIT. Do not double count gross euro sales and purchases alongside their net effect.
lessons.example: Net euro exposure before tariff is 80−50=30 million euros. A 0.10 fall in dollars per euro reduces dollar EBIT by 3 million if euro volumes, costs and timing hold. This is a transaction sensitivity, not a guarantee: local competitors, contract repricing, inventory timing, taxes and the location of cash can change the result.
lessons.transfer: Recompute downside EBIT if domestic input inflation is 3% instead of 6%, leaving all other downside inputs unchanged. Explain why a central bank rate forecast alone cannot establish the company input-cost change.

lessons.title: Test a currency hedge and a pricing response
body: A natural currency hedge exists when sales and costs share currency and timing. Meridian’s 80 million euro receipts and 50 million euro component payments leave a simplified net 30 million euro exposure. If 60% of that matched net flow, or 18 million euros, is sold forward at 1.08 dollars per euro and 12 million remains at spot, the base net dollar flow is 18×1.08+12×1.10=32.64, 0.36 below the unhedged 33. At 1.00 downside spot, the hedged net flow is 31.44, 1.44 above unhedged 30. A forward locks a rate, not the underlying customer volumes, counterparty performance or the tariff.

The tariff and domestic inflation remain in the hedge case. Holding other downside assumptions fixed, the hedge raises EBIT from 25.6 to 27.04 and net income from 8.7 to 9.78, a 1.08 after-tax improvement. The forward may also require collateral or create accounting timing differences. Before placing any hedge, treasury should reconcile net amount, invoice dates, currency of costs, credit limits and approved policy; a forecast sales amount is not the same as a committed receivable.

A naive price fix may fail. To restore 12.4 of downside EBIT with domestic revenue 120 and unchanged quantity/cost, the required extra price is 12.4/120≈10.33%. If price elasticity is −1.5 near the current price and the linear approximation is used over that increase, volume would decline by roughly 15.5%; domestic revenue becomes about 120×1.1033×.845≈111.88, below the original 120 even before cost response. This rough calculation is not a demand forecast. Run a smaller pilot with measured volumes and competitor responses rather than assuming full pass-through.
lessons.example: A hedge improves the downside dollar net euro flow by 1.44 but gives up 0.36 in the base state relative to spot. Its benefit is asymmetric across the two specified spot states, not free income. A board memo should compare operating adjustments, contractual pass-through, currency matching and limited hedging under liquidity and risk limits.
lessons.transfer: Assuming the same euro volumes and forward rate, recompute net flow if only 50% of the 30 million euro net exposure is hedged and spot is 1.00. Explain why applying the forward to gross revenue without considering imported euro costs could over-hedge.

lessons.title: From policy rates to enterprise borrowing costs
body: A central bank sets or influences short-term financing conditions but does not directly set every corporate borrowing rate. Bank margins, credit spreads, debt maturity and fixed-versus-floating debt determine transmission. Nominal cost should be distinguished from expected real cost; the approximation real rate≈nominal rate−expected inflation is unreliable for large values.

Fictional Meridian has $300M of floating-rate debt priced at a benchmark plus 2%. If the benchmark increases from 3% to 5% and outstanding principal does not change, annual interest increases from $15M to $21M, a $6M pretax cash and earnings headwind. A separate $200M fixed-rate note stays at its contractual coupon until refinancing. Do not multiply the rate change by all debt.

An executive should map reset dates, covenants, cash interest, refinancing maturities and relevant discount rates. A higher discount rate can reduce discounted project value even when operating cash flows are unchanged. Avoid assuming a rate increase always lowers nominal sales; outcomes depend on demand and currency channels.
lessons.example: Floating note: 300×(.03+.02)=15 base; 300×(.05+.02)=21 stress. Incremental annual interest=6 million. Fixed-rate notes cannot be treated as immediately repriced.
lessons.transfer: Recalculate annual interest if only 60% of the floating note reprices in the current year; explain timing and why a CFO requests a debt maturity schedule.

lessons.title: Labor markets, wages and operating leverage
body: Wage growth affects margins through headcount, hours, productivity, contract coverage, overtime and the ability to change prices. A rising unemployment rate can coincide with continuing wage pressure in specialized occupations. The CPI measures a basket of consumer prices, not the precise input inflation of an individual company.

Fictional Meridian has $200M annual labor expense, 70% of which is exposed to a negotiated 6% raise; the remainder stays unchanged. The direct cost increase is 200×.70×.06=$8.4M. An initiative improves productivity and avoids $3M of overtime, so the net cost increase is $5.4M before any implementation expense. Operating income and taxes respond differently.

Management must distinguish a productivity improvement supported by measured throughput from an optimistic budget assumption. Also consider employee turnover, defect rates, capacity constraints, and the cost of retraining. A nominal wage increase below inflation can still imply declining real wages.
lessons.example: Exposed wages=140M; increase=8.4M; verified overtime reduction=3M; net increase=5.4M. If revenue holds constant, EBIT declines 5.4M before other changes.
lessons.transfer: If a retention improvement saves another $1.2M annually but costs $0.5M to implement, quantify first-year benefit and identify whether the savings overlap with the overtime assumption.

lessons.title: Build a joint recession cash stress
body: A corporate recession plan should combine demand, cost, working capital and financing shocks rather than looking at each separately. Distinguish revenue, operating income and cash. An illustrative downturn may lower revenue, worsen customer collections, and increase credit spreads simultaneously.

Meridian sells $500M annually with variable costs of 60% of revenue and fixed operating costs of $120M. Baseline EBIT=500−300−120=$80M. A 12% volume decline with unchanged unit prices gives revenue $440M and variable cost $264M; EBIT=$56M. If a further $5M fixed operating cost increase occurs, stressed EBIT=$51M. Do not automatically assume all variable costs adjust instantly; the model makes that simplifying assumption.

Separately, if $22M of customer collections are delayed and cash expenses remain paid, the cash balance can fall $22M below the comparable case without an additional $22M reduction in recognized revenue. Liquidity planning should include minimum cash floors, debt covenants and the cost of emergency borrowing.
lessons.example: Baseline EBIT 80M. Downturn EBIT: 440−264−125=51M, down 29M. Delayed collections of 22M affect the cash forecast in addition to EBIT changes and must not be counted as an earnings loss.
lessons.transfer: Apply a 15% volume shock instead of 12%, hold fixed costs at 125M, and compute EBIT. Write one reason actual variable costs could fall less than the model predicts.

lessons.title: Inflation, rates and currency transmission
body: A currency change affects foreign sales and purchases differently; net exposures matter. Wage inflation affects exposed payroll but may be offset by evidence-based productivity improvements. A rate shock affects floating or refinancing debt, not every historical fixed coupon immediately.
Executive application: distinguish disclosed facts from hypothetical inputs. Identify a counterargument, a practical risk, and a measurable signal that would justify changing this recommendation.
lessons.example: A matched net receipt of €20M translates to $22M at 1.10 USD/EUR and $20M at 1.00 USD/EUR: $2M difference before hedges.
lessons.transfer: Recalculate the result with one changed assumption, document the effect and justify the next evidence request.

lessons.title: Scenario policies and evidence standards
body: A recession decision combines quantity, margin, working capital and financing conditions. Use a transparent economic bridge and ask whether elasticity, tax and supplier contract assumptions are causal or merely imposed. Report a leading indicator that would change the recommendation.
Executive application: distinguish disclosed facts from hypothetical inputs. Identify a counterargument, a practical risk, and a measurable signal that would justify changing this recommendation.
lessons.example: If sales drop from 500 to 450 while variable expense stays 60% and fixed costs are 120, EBIT drops from 80 to 60 million.
lessons.transfer: Recalculate the result with one changed assumption, document the effect and justify the next evidence request.

lessons.title: Rates exchange rates and debt maturity
body: Rate increases reach floating debt as contracts reset; fixed debt may be affected on refinancing. Exchange-rate moves alter translations and local competitiveness differently. A responsible economic bridge separates exposures and avoids applying one shock to every line item.
Managerial challenge: explain which input is observed versus assumed, identify a sensitivity and request the evidence necessary to act.
lessons.example: A 150-basis-point increase on $200M immediately resetting floating debt adds annual interest expense $3M, not 1.5% of every liability.
lessons.transfer: Replace a major assumption and recalculate. Explain whether your recommendation reverses and why.

lessons.title: Demand elasticity and pricing under stress
body: Pricing response requires distinguishing elasticity estimates from causal effects. A 5% price increase paired with an estimated elasticity of −1.2 suggests about 6% lower quantity under a local linear approximation, not guaranteed. Evaluate revenue, contribution and churn before action.
Managerial challenge: explain which input is observed versus assumed, identify a sensitivity and request the evidence necessary to act.
lessons.example: At price100 and quantity100, illustrative new price105 and quantity94 gives revenue9870 versus10000, down130.
lessons.transfer: Replace a major assumption and recalculate. Explain whether your recommendation reverses and why.

lessons.title: Build a board-ready numerical bridge
body: A company has €40M net annual euro inflows and $200M floating debt. USD/EUR falls from 1.10 to 1.00 and benchmark rate rises from 4% to 5.5%; margins and spread remain unchanged.
Net dollar euro flows decline from 44M to 40M, headwind 4M. Interest rises 200×.015=3M; joint pretax headwind 7M, before taxes and operations.
Reconcile each input, mark the simplifications, identify the budget, cash and governance constraints, and explain why a favorable average need not imply an acceptable downside.
lessons.example: Net dollar euro flows decline from 44M to 40M, headwind 4M. Interest rises 200×.015=3M; joint pretax headwind 7M, before taxes and operations.
lessons.transfer: Change two of the stated numerical inputs by 10% in opposite directions. Recalculate all outputs. Explain how uncertainty changes your decision.

lessons.title: Profit, resources and cash
body: The income statement measures revenue and expenses over a period. The balance sheet records assets, liabilities and equity at a date, with assets = liabilities + equity. The cash-flow statement explains the change in cash over a period through operating, investing and financing activities. Compare matching dates and scopes, including whether results are consolidated.

Accrual accounting recognizes economic activity under accounting rules rather than simply recording cash receipts and payments. A credit sale can create revenue and a receivable before collection. Buying inventory exchanges cash for an asset until the inventory is sold or otherwise expensed. Borrowing adds cash and debt without creating revenue.

Net income can increase retained earnings, but dividends and other equity changes also matter. Cash flow is not necessarily net income plus depreciation: changes in working capital and other adjustments can be material. A cash increase funded by new debt does not establish operating strength.

Ratios are starting points for questions. Current ratio compares current assets with current liabilities; quick ratio commonly excludes inventory and other less liquid current assets. An apparently strong current ratio can conceal obsolete inventory or doubtful receivables. Inspect asset composition, maturities, restrictions and footnotes before drawing a liquidity conclusion.
lessons.example: A company has cash 40, receivables 60, inventory 100 and current liabilities 100. Current ratio = 200/100 = 2.0. Using cash plus receivables only, quick ratio = 100/100 = 1.0. If 30 of receivables are doubtful, the unadjusted ratios overstate usable liquidity.
lessons.transfer: Classify a credit sale, inventory purchase and bank borrowing across statements. Explain which transactions change profit immediately under the simplified assumptions.

lessons.title: Debt capacity and refinancing
body: Debt creates contractual obligations, often with covenants and maturity dates. Leverage can amplify equity returns and losses, but a single ratio cannot establish safety. Net debt is commonly interest-bearing debt less eligible cash; define treatment of restricted cash, leases and other obligations. Different analysts may use different definitions.

Interest coverage can be defined as EBIT divided by interest expense. EBITDA coverage may look stronger but does not pay for capital expenditure, taxes or working capital. Compare cash interest, scheduled principal, maturities and minimum liquidity rather than treating EBITDA as freely available cash.

A maturity wall can make a solvent-looking company vulnerable to refinancing conditions. Fixed-rate borrowing limits near-term repricing but may still face higher rates when refinanced. Undrawn facilities can help only if committed, available and covenant-compliant. An uncommitted intention to lend is not cash.

Stress testing should connect operating decline with financing effects. A sales slowdown can reduce profit and increase receivable days while a covenant breach restricts borrowing. Independent sensitivities may understate a combined crisis. A board should monitor headroom and escalation triggers before a payment failure.
lessons.example: Debt 300, eligible cash 50, EBITDA 100 gives net debt 250 and net-debt/EBITDA 2.5×. EBIT 60 and interest 15 give coverage 4×. If EBIT falls to 30 and interest rises to 20, coverage falls to 1.5×. Neither ratio shows whether a 100 debt maturity next month can be paid.
lessons.transfer: Create a liquidity table with opening cash, operating receipts, payments, capex, debt service and minimum reserve. Explain the difference between committed and assumed refinancing.

lessons.title: Read beyond the headline
body: Begin a disclosure review with the reporting period, currency, accounting framework and audit status. Read the primary statements alongside notes, segment disclosures, accounting policies and management discussion. An adjusted metric should be reconciled to the reported measure, with a clear definition and reason for adjustments.

Look for divergence between earnings and cash, unusually fast receivables growth, repeated “one-time” exclusions, changes in estimates and dependence on financing. These are questions for investigation, not proof of misconduct. Acquisitions, seasonality and deliberate inventory investment can create legitimate divergences.

Assess comparability. A change in accounting scope, acquired business or fiscal calendar can affect apparent growth. Separate organic change from structural change where data permit. Do not silently compare a quarterly flow with an annual flow or a year-end balance with an average balance.

A useful disclosure review identifies what is known, what is estimated and what cannot be concluded from public information. Cite sections and preserve calculation trails. A recommendation should be conditional when crucial details are missing; avoid treating a summary ratio as a substitute for notes and contracts.
lessons.example: Revenue grows 10% while receivables grow 40%. This may indicate slower collections, acquisition effects, mix or timing. If net income is 70 but operating cash flow 20 and capex 35, simple free cash flow is −15. Request a working-capital bridge and explanation of material adjustments before judging performance.
lessons.transfer: Draft five questions for a CFO whose adjusted profit rises while operating cash flow falls. Include one benign explanation you would test.

lessons.title: Earnings-to-cash bridge and estimate challenge
body: Operating cash flow under the indirect method begins with net income and adjusts for noncash items and operating balance changes. Add depreciation; subtract receivables and inventory increases; add operating payable increases, subject to acquisition, currency and classification effects. A bridge that balances is still only an arithmetic reconciliation; it cannot establish that revenue was valid or customers can pay.

Compare receivables with credit sales over matching periods. A rise in days sales outstanding can reflect weak collections, deliberate terms, acquisition, seasonality or an accounting estimate; investigate aging, customer concentration, credit losses and contracts. Never infer misconduct from a single ratio. An aggressive useful-life extension may lift profit without adding cash or changing replacement needs.

Quality-of-earnings analysis asks what normalized, repeatable cash generation looks like. Disclose adjustments rather than accepting management’s adjusted metric at face value. Analyze working-capital releases separately from sustainable operating margins. Request source footnotes and management explanation for both favorable and adverse deviations.
lessons.example: Fictional consolidated net income 120, depreciation 30, receivables +45, inventory +20 and payables +15 imply simplified operating cash 100. With capex 70, simple FCF is 30. If 15 of cash came from stretching suppliers beyond sustainable terms, normalized near-term cash is lower; this is a sensitivity, not a required accounting adjustment to the published statement.
lessons.transfer: Build a bridge when receivables instead increase 65 and payables remain 15. Explain what evidence would test whether the 20 difference is seasonal or persistent.

lessons.title: Covenant headroom and the debt maturity wall
body: Debt analysis requires both amount and timing. A covenant may cap net-debt-to-EBITDA or demand minimum interest coverage under definitions in an agreement. Those definitions may adjust EBITDA, restrict eligible cash or set measurement dates. A ratio calculated from a summary press release is not proof of compliance. State the exact assumed definitions for classroom cases.

Headroom is the distance to a limit. A firm at 2.5× net leverage with a 3.0× maximum has numerical headroom, but lower EBITDA or borrowing can erase it. Compare cash needed for maturities, capex and minimum operating reserve with committed facilities. A facility subject to covenant compliance may become less usable precisely when needed.

Build a quarterly cash calendar. Annual operating cash flow may arrive after a principal payment. Stress collections and margin together, then state which management actions are actually discretionary. A plan to refinance is a hypothesis until it is committed. Changing accounting estimates to improve covenant EBITDA without economic improvement is not a funding solution.
lessons.example: Assume debt 500, eligible cash 100, covenant EBITDA 160 and max net-debt/EBITDA 3.0×. Net leverage=400/160=2.5×. If EBITDA falls to 130 with debt and cash unchanged, ratio=3.077×, breaching the assumed limit. The minimum EBITDA for compliance is 400/3≈133.33. A 120 maturity due next quarter still requires a cash calendar even in the base ratio case.
lessons.transfer: If cash falls 30 to fund capex while debt stays 500 and EBITDA 160, recalculate leverage and discuss whether funding capex from cash creates covenant risk.

lessons.title: Segment disclosures and executive forecast challenge
body: Consolidated ratios can conceal a weak segment offset by a strong one. Read the segment note for revenue, profit definition, intersegment transfers and assets before ranking divisions. Some public reports omit comparable invested capital or use management-defined segment profit; do not fabricate an ROIC from incompatible measures.

A credible forecast starts from operating drivers: volume, price, mix, cost and investment by segment. Link revenue and margins to receivables, inventory, capex and debt service. If a forecast assumes sales growth and faster collections, test whether customer terms or mix justify both. An adverse scenario may affect several drivers at once.

Present a board recommendation with a reconciled group total, segment downside, funding needs and a monitorable trigger. Explain what cannot be inferred without contract detail or cash timing. Compare remedies—collections, pricing, inventory and financing—on service quality and reversibility. Even a well-labeled ratio cannot replace source disclosure.
lessons.example: Segment A revenue 600 and operating profit 90; segment B revenue 400 and profit 20. Corporate unallocated expense 30 yields consolidated operating profit 80 on revenue 1,000, or 8%. A and B margins are 15% and 5%; their weighted combined margin before corporate cost is 11%. An unweighted average 10% is wrong, and neither segment margin reconciles group profit without 30 corporate expense.
lessons.transfer: If B revenue falls 10% at unchanged 5% segment margin while A and corporate expense remain fixed, compute group margin and challenge the constant-margin assumption.

lessons.title: Reconcile earnings to cash before judging quality
body: Net income is an accrual measure, while operating cash flow starts with earnings and reconciles noncash charges and working-capital changes. An increase in receivables means sales recognized before collection and is subtracted in the indirect cash-flow bridge; an increase in inventory uses cash; an increase in payables temporarily supplies cash. Compare balance-sheet changes with the cash-flow statement, accounting-policy notes and acquisitions or foreign exchange before attributing every change to operations.

Free cash flow has multiple definitions. For a transparent screening measure, state CFO less cash capital expenditure; do not call this the same as unlevered free cash flow to the firm when CFO includes interest and tax. Distinguish maintenance from growth capex only when disclosures support it. A positive net-income trend can coexist with deteriorating collections, and a one-time working-capital release can make CFO look temporarily strong.

A senior-executive memo should explain the mechanism, not just quote a ratio. Ask whether receivable days rose because of customer mix, extended terms, cut-off errors or a seasonal acquisition. Reconcile annual and interim periods with the same denominator; investigate material noncash gains, supplier financing and restricted cash rather than assuming all reported cash is available for debt service.
lessons.example: Fictional Apex reports net income 75, depreciation 45, receivables up 35, inventory up 20 and payables up 10, with no other operating adjustments. CFO = 75+45−35−20+10 = 75. Cash capex 70 gives a clearly defined CFO-minus-capex proxy of 5. If 25 of the receivable increase is delayed payment from one customer, that is a collection hypothesis requiring invoice-aging evidence, not a proved fact.
lessons.transfer: Recompute CFO if receivables rose 50 rather than 35, and explain why an acquisition could break the simple balance-sheet-change bridge.

lessons.title: Translate credit ratios into a liquidity decision
body: A covenant is a contract-defined test, not a universal financial ratio. Begin with the actual agreement definition of EBITDA, permitted add-backs, debt, cash netting, measurement date and cure rights. An illustrative net-leverage ratio divides eligible net debt by eligible EBITDA; headroom is the permitted maximum minus the measured ratio. Interest coverage divides an agreed earnings measure by specified interest expense, with a minimum rather than a maximum threshold.

In a simplified Apex screening case, EBIT 120 plus depreciation 45 gives EBITDA 165; debt 400 less available cash 60 gives net debt 340. At interest 20, net leverage is 340/165 ≈ 2.06× and EBITDA/interest is 8.25×. If a fictional agreement caps net leverage at 3.0× and requires coverage of 4.0×, both pass in this illustrative calculation. The actual contract may net less cash or exclude some earnings.

Stress simultaneous shocks. If EBIT falls to 60, depreciation remains 45, debt rises to 460 while cash stays 60, and annual interest rises to 30, EBITDA is 105, net debt 400, leverage ≈ 3.81×, and coverage 3.50×. Both illustrative thresholds fail. A covenant test does not itself predict the date cash runs out; build a monthly cash waterfall with maturities, revolver availability, minimum operating cash and remediation options.
lessons.example: At base net debt 340 and EBITDA 165, the 3.0× cap permits at most 495 net debt, or 155 headroom if EBITDA holds. In the stressed state with net debt 400, EBITDA must be at least 400/3 ≈ 133.33 to satisfy leverage; the assumed 105 misses by 28.33. At 30 interest, coverage ≥4 requires EBITDA ≥120, which also fails. These thresholds are algebraic, not forecasts.
lessons.transfer: At base net debt 340, find the smallest EBITDA that passes a 3.0× cap. Explain why a rolling-four-quarter test may fail before a full-year cash budget does.

lessons.title: Cash-flow bridge and working capital
body: A profitable company may be underfunded if receivables rise faster than collections. Start with net income, add noncash expenses, then adjust for changes in operating working capital. Define cash flow and capital expenditure conventions consistently.
Executive application: distinguish disclosed facts from hypothetical inputs. Identify a counterargument, a practical risk, and a measurable signal that would justify changing this recommendation.
lessons.example: Net income 90, noncash depreciation 20, receivables increase 15 and payables increase 5: simple CFO=90+20−15+5=100 million.
lessons.transfer: Recalculate the result with one changed assumption, document the effect and justify the next evidence request.

lessons.title: Debt covenants and investment choices
body: A ratio test is only as reliable as its legal definition. Net debt/EBITDA may use adjusted EBITDA, restricted cash and permitted acquisition addbacks. A board memo must distinguish published accounting results, permitted covenant adjustments, and management's own forecasts.
Executive application: distinguish disclosed facts from hypothetical inputs. Identify a counterargument, a practical risk, and a measurable signal that would justify changing this recommendation.
lessons.example: If disclosed net debt 450 and comparable EBITDA 150, illustrative net leverage is 3.0x, before any indenture-defined adjustment.
lessons.transfer: Recalculate the result with one changed assumption, document the effect and justify the next evidence request.

lessons.title: Debt maturity walls and covenant headroom
body: Cash availability is different from reported profit. A treasury review maps unrestricted cash, revolving facility availability, collateral requirements and debt repayments by date. Covenant calculations follow governing agreement definitions, not assumed accounting ratios.
Managerial challenge: explain which input is observed versus assumed, identify a sensitivity and request the evidence necessary to act.
lessons.example: An illustrative $50M cash balance less $20M minimum operating cash leaves $30M before debt repayment and facility restrictions.
lessons.transfer: Replace a major assumption and recalculate. Explain whether your recommendation reverses and why.

lessons.title: Earnings quality and cash-flow reconciliation
body: Operating cash flow begins with earnings and adjusts noncash items and changes in working capital. Rising receivables are a cash use. Executives need a bridge of changes in earnings, cash conversion and investments, including acquisition and financing classifications.
Managerial challenge: explain which input is observed versus assumed, identify a sensitivity and request the evidence necessary to act.
lessons.example: Net income 65, depreciation 12, receivables rise 18 and payables rise 6: simplified CFO=65+12−18+6=65M.
lessons.transfer: Replace a major assumption and recalculate. Explain whether your recommendation reverses and why.

lessons.title: Build a board-ready numerical bridge
body: CFO before collections shock is $150M, capex $90M, collection delay $25M. Assume delay is a current-year CFO reduction and no other cash changes.
Revised CFO=125M. Simplified free cash flow after shock=125−90=35M; before shock=60M. Delayed collection is a working-capital cash effect, not automatically another revenue loss.
Reconcile each input, mark the simplifications, identify the budget, cash and governance constraints, and explain why a favorable average need not imply an acceptable downside.
lessons.example: Revised CFO=125M. Simplified free cash flow after shock=125−90=35M; before shock=60M. Delayed collection is a working-capital cash effect, not automatically another revenue loss.
lessons.transfer: Change two of the stated numerical inputs by 10% in opposite directions. Recalculate all outputs. Explain how uncertainty changes your decision.

lessons.title: Reconcile an enterprise-wide strategic decision
body: Fictional Atlas Group has three divisions and is considering expansion while interest rates rise. Executives must first reconcile operating returns with capital employed, and then assess projects using cash-flow timing, working capital and financing constraints. A profitable project can still be unaffordable during a credit squeeze.

Use income statements to calculate EBIT and NOPAT; reconcile CFO using noncash expenses and working capital; calculate a consistent CFO-minus-capex measure; and distinguish financial accounting from operational forecasts. The board should demand alternative projects and a correlated downside involving revenue, costs and the financing rate.

This integrated case is an independently authored teaching exercise. It is not a university exam, and the attached quantitative examination is automatically graded while the board memo is self-reviewed.
lessons.example: Revenue 600, variable costs 55% and fixed costs 180 imply EBIT 90. A 10% sales drop with the same variable-cost rate gives EBIT 63. This $27M change is the operating leverage effect under the simplified assumptions.
lessons.transfer: Build a combined downside with the $27M EBIT change, $3.75M extra debt interest on $250M of floating debt after a 150-bp shock, and delayed customer receipts of $20M. Explain earnings versus cash impacts without double-counting.
